description: Siloscape is malware that targets Kubernetes clusters through Windows containers. Siloscape was first observed in March 2021.

output.snippet:
Siloscape searches for the Kubernetes config file and other related files using a regular expression.
Siloscape can run cmd through an IRC channel.
Siloscape searches for the kubec
macOS.OSAMiner has used `curl` to download a Stripped Payloads from a public facing adversary-controlled webpage.

A FinFisher variant uses a custom packer.
FinFisher probes the system to check for antimalware processes.

WannaCry uses Tor for command and control traffic.
WannaCry uses Tor for command and control traffic and routes a custom cryptographic protocol over the Tor circuit.
WannaCry will
WannaCry utilizes wmic to delete shadow copies. WannaCry uses vssadmin, wbadmin, bcdedit, and wmic to delete and di
In older versions, XCSSET uses the plutil command to modify the LSUIElement, DFBundleDisplayName, and CFBundleIdentifier keys in
SystemBC has used DNS servers to resolve .bit domains to C2 infrastructure.

PUNCHTRACK is loaded and executed by a highly obfuscated launcher.
PUNCHTRACK scrapes memory for properly formatted payment card data.
SpeakUp can perform brute forcing using a pre-defined list of usernames and passwords in an attempt to log in to administrative panels. SpeakUp uses the arp -a command

Azorult can collect the time zone information from the system.
Azorult can capture screenshots of the victim’s machines.
Azorult uses an XOR key to decrypt content and uses Base64

KeyBoy time-stomped its DLL in order to evade detection.
KeyBoy uses the Dynamic Data Exchange (DDE) protocol to download remote payloads.
KeyBoy can determine the public or WAN IP

BRUSHFIRE has monitored inbound VPN traffic to compromised appliances until specific inbound packets contain a specific magic string/pattern instead of external beaconing.
BRUSHFIR

ref-0953b5a880a40aa15654.text:
BRUSHFIRE has monitored inbound VPN traffic to compromised appliances until specific inbound packets contain a specific magic string/pattern instead of external beaconing.
BRUSHFIRE has the ability to exfiltrate data on-demand through executing commands obtained via monitoring for specially crafted packets and sending output back in an embedded SSL response.
ref-0953b5a880a40aa15654.title: Sila Ozeren Hacioglu. (2025, May 5). UNC5221’s Latest Exploit: Weaponizing CVE-2025-22457 in Ivanti Connect Secure. Retrieved April 13, 2026.

ref-1546bbc2280a29223eed.text: In older versions, XCSSET uses the plutil command to modify the LSUIElement, DFBundleDisplayName, and CFBundleIdentifier keys in the /Contents/Info.plist file to change how XCSSET is visible on the system. In later versions, XCSSET leverages a third-party notarized `dockutil` tool to modify the `.plist` file responsible for presenting applications to the user in the Dock and LaunchPad to point to a malicious application. XCSSET uses scp to access the ~/Library/Cookies/Cookies.binarycookies file. XCSSET uses ps aux with the grep command to enumerate common browsers and system processes potentially impacting XCSSET's exfiltration capabilities. XCSSET loads a system level launchdaemon using the launchctl load -w command from /System/Librarby/LaunchDaemons/ssh.plist. XCSSET prompts the user to input credentials using a native macOS dialog box leveraging the system process /Applications/Safari.app/Contents/MacOS/SafariForWebKitDevelopment. XCSSET uses a shell script to execute Mach-o files and osacompile commands such as, osacompile -x -o xcode.app main.applescript. XCSSET uses the ssh launchdaemon to elevate privileges, bypass system controls, and enable remote access to the victim. XCSSET uses AppleScript to check the host's language and location with the command user locale of (get system info). XCSSET installs malicious application bundles that mimic native macOS apps, such as Safari, by using the legitimate app’s icon and customizing the `Info.plist` to match expected metadata. XCSSET collects contacts and application data from files in Desktop, Documents, Downloads, Dropbox, and WeChat folders. XCSSET identifies the macOS version and uses ioreg to determine serial number. XCSSET adds malicious code to a host's Xcode projects by enumerating CocoaPods target_integrator.rb files under the /Library/Ruby/Gems folder or enumerates all .xcodeproj folders under a given directory. XCSSET then downloads a script and Mach-O file into the Xcode project folder. XCSSET performs AES-CBC encryption on files under ~/Documents, ~/Downloads, and ~/Desktop with a fixed key and renames files to give them a .enc extension. Only files with sizes less than 500MB are encrypted. XCSSET uses a hidden folder named .xcassets and .git to embed itself in Xcode. XCSSET uses a malicious browser application to replace the legitimate browser in order to continuously capture credentials, monitor web traffic, and download additional modules. XCSSET searches firewall configuration files located in /Library/Preferences/ and uses csrutil status to determine if System Integrity Protection is enabled. XCSSET adds malicious file paths to the DYLD_FRAMEWORK_PATH and DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH environment variables to execute malicious code. XCSSET retrieves files that match the pattern defined in the INAME_QUERY variable within the user's home directory, such as `*test.txt`, and are below a specific size limit. It then archives the files and exfiltrates the data over its C2 channel. XCSSET downloads browser specific AppleScript modules using a constructed URL with the curl command, https://" & domain & "/agent/scripts/" & moduleName & ".applescript. XCSSET attempts to discover accounts from various locations such as a user's Evernote, AppleID, Telegram, Skype, and WeChat data. XCSSET will create an ssh key if necessary with the ssh-keygen -t rsa -f $HOME/.ssh/id_rsa -P command. XCSSET will upload a private key file to the server to remotely access the host without a password. Using the machine's local time, XCSSET waits 43200 seconds (12 hours) from the initial creation timestamp of a specific file, .report. After the elapsed time, XCSSET executes additional modules. XCSSET saves a screen capture of the victim's system with a numbered filename and .jpg extension. Screen captures are taken at specified intervals based on the system. XCSSET uses RC4 encryption over TCP to communicate with its C2 server. XCSSET will compress entire ~/Desktop folders excluding all .git folders, but only if the total data size is under 200MB. XCSSET has used a zero-day exploit in the ssh launchdaemon to elevate privileges and bypass SIP.
ref-1546bbc2280a29223eed.title: Mac Threat Response, Mobile Research Team. (2020, August 13). The XCSSET Malware: Inserts Malicious Code Into Xcode Projects, Performs UXSS Backdoor Planting in Safari, and Leverages Two Zero-day Exploits. Retrieved October 5, 2021.

ref-2e5ce0b63b29a50bf2af.text: Raspberry Robin uses rundll32 execution without any command line parameters to contact command and control infrastructure, such as IP addresses associated with Tor nodes. Raspberry Robin retrieves its second stage payload in a variety of ways such as through msiexec.exe abuse, or running the curl command to download the payload to the victim's %AppData% folder. Raspberry Robin uses newly-registered domains containing only a few characters for command and controll purposes, such as "v0[.]cx". Raspberry Robin uses regsvr32.exe execution without any command line parameters for command and control requests to IP addresses associated with Tor nodes. Raspberry Robin uses mixed-case letters for filenames and commands to evade detection. Raspberry Robin uses msiexec.exe for post-installation communication to command and control infrastructure. Msiexec.exe is executed referencing a remote resource for second-stage payload retrieval and execution. Raspberry Robin uses the Windows utility odbcconf.exe to execute malicious commands, using the regsvr flag to execute DLLs and bypass application control mechanisms that are not monitoring for odbcconf.exe abuse. Raspberry Robin is capable of contacting the TOR network for delivering second-stage payloads. Raspberry Robin has historically been delivered via infected USB drives containing a malicious LNK object masquerading as a legitimate folder. Raspberry Robin uses cmd.exe to read and execute a file stored on an infected USB device as part of initial installation. Raspberry Robin will communicate via HTTP over port 8080 for command and control traffic. Raspberry Robin uses outbound HTTP requests containing victim information for retrieving second stage payloads. Variants of Raspberry Robin can download archive files (such as 7-Zip files) via the victim web browser for second stage execution. Raspberry Robin has historically used infected USB media to spread to new victims. Raspberry Robin will use the legitimate Windows utility fodhelper.exe to run processes at elevated privileges without requiring a User Account Control prompt.
ref-2e5ce0b63b29a50bf2af.title: Lauren Podber and Stef Rand. (2022, May 5). Raspberry Robin gets the worm early. Retrieved May 17, 2024.

ref-8078a6bdb34a10246c85.text: Cobalt Strike can conduct peer-to-peer communication over Windows named pipes encapsulated in the SMB protocol. All protocols use their standard assigned ports. Cobalt Strike has the ability to use an Excel Workbook to execute additional code by enabling Office to trust macros and execute code without user permission. Cobalt Strike can use self signed Java applets to execute signed applet attacks. Cobalt Strike's Beacon payload can collect information on process details. Cobalt Strike uses the native Windows Network Enumeration APIs to interrogate and discover targets in a Windows Active Directory network. Cobalt Strike has the ability to use AES-256 symmetric encryption in CBC mode with HMAC-SHA-256 to encrypt task commands and XOR to encrypt shell code and configuration data. Cobalt Strike can query HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Office\\Excel\Security\AccessVBOM\ to determine if the security setting for restricting default programmatic access is enabled. Cobalt Strike can perform port scans from an infected host. Cobalt Strike has the ability to load DLLs via reflective injection. Cobalt Strike can exploit Oracle Java vulnerabilities for execution, including CVE-2011-3544, CVE-2013-2465, CVE-2012-4681, and CVE-2013-2460. Cobalt Strike can produce a sessions report from compromised hosts. Cobalt Strike can hash functions to obfuscate calls to the Windows API and use a public/private key pair to encrypt Beacon session metadata. Cobalt Strike uses a command-line interface to interact with systems. The Cobalt Strike System Profiler can use JavaScript to perform reconnaissance actions. Cobalt Strike can deliver additional payloads to victim machines. Cobalt Strike can use RSA asymmetric encryption with PKCS1 padding to encrypt data sent to the C2 server. Cobalt Strike can be configured to use TCP, ICMP, and UDP for C2 communications. Cobalt Strike can use a custom command and control protocol that can be encapsulated in DNS. All protocols use their standard assigned ports. Cobalt Strike can modify Registry values within HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Office\\Excel\Security\AccessVBOM\ to enable the execution of additional code. Cobalt Strike can download a hosted "beacon" payload using BITSAdmin. Cobalt Strike has the ability to use Smart Applet attacks to disable the Java SecurityManager sandbox.
ref-8078a6bdb34a10246c85.title: Mavis, N. (2020, September 21). The Art and Science of Detecting Cobalt Strike. Retrieved September 12, 2024.

ref-86e2a5c32e017691a8a5.text:
PUNCHTRACK is loaded and executed by a highly obfuscated launcher.
PUNCHTRACK scrapes memory for properly formatted payment card data.
ref-86e2a5c32e017691a8a5.title: Kizhakkinan, D., et al. (2016, May 11). Threat Actor Leverages Windows Zero-day Exploit in Payment Card Data Attacks. Retrieved February 12, 2018.

ref-94a50723256e044e5044.text: Azorult can collect the time zone information from the system. Azorult can capture screenshots of the victim’s machines. Azorult uses an XOR key to decrypt content and uses Base64 to decode the C2 address. Azorult can steal credentials in files belonging to common software such as Skype, Telegram, and Steam. Azorult can call WTSQueryUserToken and CreateProcessAsUser to start a new process with local system privileges. Azorult can decrypt the payload into memory, create a new suspended process of itself, then inject a decrypted payload to the new process and resume new process execution. Azorult can collect the username from the victim’s machine. Azorult can download and execute additional files. Azorult has also downloaded a ransomware payload called Hermes. Azorult can steal credentials from the victim's browser. Azorult can collect a list of running processes by calling CreateToolhelp32Snapshot. Azorult can recursively search for files in folders and collects files from the desktop with certain extensions. Azorult can collect host IP information from the victim’s machine. Azorult can check for installed software on the system under the Registry key Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall. Azorult can delete files from victim machines. Azorult can encrypt C2 traffic using XOR. Azorult can collect the machine information, system architecture, the OS version, computer name, Windows product name, the number of CPU cores, video card information, and the system language.
ref-94a50723256e044e5044.title: Yan, T., et al. (2018, November 21). New Wine in Old Bottle: New Azorult Variant Found in FindMyName Campaign using Fallout Exploit Kit. Retrieved November 29, 2018.

ref-a92ec48c6a803109c78b.text: KeyBoy time-stomped its DLL in order to evade detection. KeyBoy uses the Dynamic Data Exchange (DDE) protocol to download remote payloads. KeyBoy can determine the public or WAN IP address for the system. KeyBoy uses custom SSL libraries to impersonate SSL in C2 traffic. KeyBoy uses -w Hidden to conceal a PowerShell window that downloads a payload. KeyBoy has a command to perform screen grabbing. KeyBoy uses PowerShell commands to download and execute payloads. KeyBoy has a command to launch a file browser or explorer on the system.
ref-a92ec48c6a803109c78b.title: Parys, B. (2017, February 11). The KeyBoys are back in town. Retrieved June 13, 2019.

ref-ba036217b9af5c3654a0.text: WannaCry utilizes wmic to delete shadow copies. WannaCry uses vssadmin, wbadmin, bcdedit, and wmic to delete and disable operating system recovery features. WannaCry creates the service "mssecsvc2.0" with the display name "Microsoft Security Center (2.0) Service." WannaCry uses attrib +h and icacls . /grant Everyone:F /T /C /Q to make some of its files hidden and grant all users full access controls. WannaCry uses an exploit in SMBv1 to spread itself to other remote systems on a network. WannaCry enumerates current remote desktop sessions and tries to execute the malware on each session. WannaCry searches for variety of user files by file extension before encrypting them using RSA and AES, including Office, PDF, image, audio, video, source code, archive/compression format, and key and certificate files. WannaCry encrypts user files and demands that a ransom be paid in Bitcoin to decrypt those files. WannaCry attempts to copy itself to remote computers after gaining access via an SMB exploit.
ref-ba036217b9af5c3654a0.title: Noerenberg, E., Costis, A., and Quist, N. (2017, May 16). A Technical Analysis of WannaCry Ransomware. Retrieved December 8, 2024.

ref-c5d37c7ffa310d5ed8c5.text: SystemBC has used DNS servers to resolve .bit domains to C2 infrastructure.
ref-c5d37c7ffa310d5ed8c5.title: Harmon, K., et al. (2019, August 1). SystemBC is like Christmas in July for SOCKS5 Malware and Exploit Kits . Retrieved June 13, 2025.

ref-cfbe3ef44c89024da699.text:
A FinFisher variant uses a custom packer.
FinFisher probes the system to check for antimalware processes.
ref-cfbe3ef44c89024da699.title: Kaspersky Lab's Global Research & Analysis Team. (2017, October 16). BlackOasis APT and new targeted attacks leveraging zero-day exploit. Retrieved February 15, 2018.

ref-d011777dbd2fc6ae6202.text: macOS.OSAMiner has used `curl` to download a Stripped Payloads from a public facing adversary-controlled webpage.
ref-d011777dbd2fc6ae6202.title: MITRE ATT&CK software S1048

ref-ed9fd713821239dc3ad8.text: SpeakUp can perform brute forcing using a pre-defined list of usernames and passwords in an attempt to log in to administrative panels. SpeakUp uses the arp -a command. SpeakUp uses Python scripts. SpeakUp uses cron tasks to ensure persistence. SpeakUp uses POST and GET requests over HTTP to communicate with its main C&C server. SpeakUp encodes C&C communication using Base64. SpeakUp encodes its second-stage payload with Base64. SpeakUp uses Perl scripts. SpeakUp attempts to exploit the following vulnerabilities in order to execute its malicious script: CVE-2012-0874, CVE-2010-1871, CVE-2017-10271, CVE-2018-2894, CVE-2016-3088, JBoss AS 3/4/5/6, and the Hadoop YARN ResourceManager. SpeakUp uses the ifconfig -a command. SpeakUp deletes files to remove evidence on the machine. SpeakUp uses the whoami command. SpeakUp checks for availability of specific ports on servers. SpeakUp uses the cat /proc/cpuinfo | grep -c “cpu family” 2>&1 command to gather system information. SpeakUp downloads and executes additional files from a remote server.
ref-ed9fd713821239dc3ad8.title: Check Point Research. (2019, February 4). SpeakUp: A New Undetected Backdoor Linux Trojan. Retrieved April 17, 2019.

ref-ee80c154798ce36b2a0d.text: Siloscape searches for the Kubernetes config file and other related files using a regular expression. Siloscape can run cmd through an IRC channel. Siloscape searches for the kubectl binary. Siloscape has decrypted the password of the C2 server with a simple byte by byte XOR. Siloscape also writes both an archive of Tor and the unzip binary to disk from data embedded within the payload using Visual Studio’s Resource Manager. Siloscape uses Tor to communicate with C2. Siloscape checks for Kubernetes node permissions. Siloscape can send kubectl commands to victim clusters through an IRC channel and can run kubectl locally to spread once within a victim cluster. Siloscape has leveraged a vulnerability in Windows containers to perform an Escape to Host. Siloscape is executed after the attacker gains initial access to a Windows container using a known vulnerability. Siloscape impersonates the main thread of CExecSvc.exe by calling NtImpersonateThread. Siloscape maps the host’s C drive to the container by creating a global symbolic link to the host through the calling of NtSetInformationSymbolicLink. Siloscape makes various native API calls. Siloscape itself is obfuscated and uses obfuscated API calls. Siloscape connects to an IRC server for C2.
ref-ee80c154798ce36b2a0d.title: Prizmant, D. (2021, June 7). Siloscape: First Known Malware Targeting Windows Containers to Compromise Cloud Environments. Retrieved June 9, 2021.
